analysis.one_liner: Adds cost-benefit, hearing, and court-review hurdles that make major federal regulations harder to issue.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee with zero cosponsors until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the procedures federal agencies must follow when writing major rules — the regulations that implement laws on clean air, workplace safety, food and drug safety, financial protection, and more. It would require agencies to prove a rule maximizes quantified benefits over costs, let affected companies petition for trial-like hearings with cross-examination, give the White House regulatory office (OIRA) a gatekeeping role before any proposed rule is published, and make major rules easier to overturn in court. It was introduced in September 2022, referred to the Judiciary Committee and a subcommittee, and never moved again before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Large regulated corporations and their trade associations benefit most if it passes: every added procedural step — advance notices, 90-day comment periods, formal hearings, and stricter court review — is a point where a well-funded company can slow, weaken, or litigate away a rule it dislikes. Regulatory law firms benefit from the added litigation. The White House regulatory office (OIRA) gains new statutory power over every agency's rulemaking.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large regulated corporations and trade associations

how_it_helps.text: For major rules (those costing $100 million or more) the agency must adopt the alternative that maximizes net benefits within the authorizing statute unless OIRA approves otherwise, giving regulated parties a statutory hook to challenge any costlier protective rule.

For high-impact rules (those with $500 million or more in annual economic effects), any interested person can petition for a formal public hearing with oral presentations, cross-examination, and the burden of proof on the agency proposing the rule.
Agencies cannot publish a proposed rule until the OIRA Administrator concludes review, and the bill shields OIRA's own rulemaking-review actions from judicial review.

The bill widens the grounds for overturning rules in court: for high-impact rules, courts must check the agency's factual findings against a 'substantial evidence' standard, and it directs how much deference courts give agency interpretations.

It also requires advance notice before major rulemakings, longer comment periods (90 days for major rules, plus a 30-day responsive comment round), public dockets for the science and data behind rules, and periodic retrospective reviews of major rules.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people bear the cost indirectly: the rules this process governs are the ones that limit pollution, enforce workplace and product safety, and police financial misconduct, so each added step of delay, analysis, and litigation postpones or dilutes those protections. Taxpayers also fund the expanded agency analyses, dockets, and reviews, and agencies divert staff time from writing rules to defending them.

drawbacks.text: Trial-like hearings with cross-examination and an agency burden of proof are expensive and slow; the heaviest users of such processes would be well-resourced companies, and the added timelines (a 90-day advance notice, 90-day comment periods, a 30-day response round) can postpone health, safety, and environmental protections for years.

Requiring agencies to adopt the rule that maximizes net benefits within the authorizing statute can systematically shortchange protections whose benefits — saved lives, cleaner air, avoided fraud — are real but hard to put a dollar figure on, even though the bill does allow an exception for unquantifiable benefits if OIRA approves.

The bill bars agencies from publicly advocating for their own proposed rules or encouraging public comment on them, which can leave agency proposals contested in the public record mainly by organized industry commenters.

A good-faith case for the bill exists: public dockets, longer comment periods, responsiveness requirements, and mandatory reviews of whether old rules still work would make rulemaking more transparent and accountable, and cost-benefit discipline can weed out poorly designed rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency and retrospective-review pieces have genuine value, but they are paired with mechanisms — the net-benefits mandate, formal hearings, and stricter court review — whose practical effect is to shift advantage in rulemaking toward parties with the money to sustain multi-year proceedings and litigation. Weighed honestly, the bill would trade some procedural openness for a system in which major public protections are slower, easier to challenge, and easier to water down; the benefits are real but smaller and more diffuse than the costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on September 9, 2022, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then sent to a subcommittee on November 1, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Beth Van Duyne introduced the Regulatory Accountability Act on September 9, 2022, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
On November 1, 2022, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law, where it remained with no further action.
No member cosponsored the bill, and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died quietly, the existing rulemaking procedures and the public protections that flow through them stayed in place; regulated industries gained nothing but also lost nothing, and agencies were spared the new procedural burden.

for.name: Rep. Beth Van Duyne
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 9, 2022; no other member cosponsored it.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

against.name: Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 1, 2022 and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no Democrat signed on, so the partisan shape was never tested; the bill's only sponsor was a Republican with zero cosponsors of either party.

industries.industry: Large regulated corporations (energy, chemical, manufacturing, finance)
industries.note: The bill creates multiple chokepoints — advance notices, extended comment rounds, formal hearings, and easier court challenges — where a well-funded regulated company can delay or defeat a rule. Those delays shift the cost of unresolved pollution, safety, and financial risks onto the public.

Substantial-evidence review of high-impact rules and expanded hearing procedures generate more litigation against federal rules. The firms that profit from that work are paid by parties contesting the rules, not by the people the rules protect.

industries.industry: Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (White House regulatory review office)
industries.note: The bill makes OIRA review a formal, mandatory step before any proposed rule is published and writes its cost-benefit role into statute, centralizing power over every agency's rulemaking. Whether that serves the public depends entirely on which administration holds the office.
